newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Many Swedish groups ponders share list change-poll.
newsitem.headline: Many Swedish groups ponders share list change-poll.

text.p: Almost half of companies listed on the Stockholm Stock Exchange's main A list are considering moving to the smaller O list for tax reasons, a poll by Skandinavisk opinion ab (SKOP) showed on Friday.
The poll, commissioned and published by the Swedish Association for Share Promotion, showed 42 percent of companies on the A list were considering a transfer.
The survey also said the new wealth tax had made 12 percent of Swedish companies more interested in moving headquarters abroad.

A 1996 law forces Swedes with wealth exceeding 900,000 crowns to pay 1.5 percent tax on 100 percent of the value of shares listed on the A list, up from 75 percent, while shares on the smaller O list remain exempt from tax.

The law has caused companies such as fashion retailer Hennes & Mauritz, media group Marieberg AB, construction group Lundbergs and investment companies Latour and Custos to flee from the A to the O list this month.

The recent share transfers were triggered by a law adopted by parliament in June reaffirming that main shareholders -- people holding more than 25 percent of votes -- have to pay tax for shares listed on the A list before 1991.
Companies that started trading on the A list before 1991 had hoped parliament would change the 1996 law.
Some Swedish companies, among them telecoms giant Ericsson, have previously said they are considering to move their headquarters abroad, citing a poor business climate and high tax pressure.
"The survey shows how seriously bourse companies view the new wealth tax," the Association for Share Promotion said.
"The government has to withdraw its proposal."

On Wednesday, Sweden's Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said he did not rule out a change in wealth tax for main owners of companies listed on the bourse's primary A list but added no mesaures were currently on the agenda.
He said the government did not intend to impose wealth tax on the bourse's smaller lists.
On Friday Swedish daily Finanstidningen reported that the Centre Party, the ruling Social Democrats informal cooperation partner, was discussing wealth tax changes with the government.
"We have started such talks now," Centre Party group chairman Per-Ola Eriksson told the newspaper. "We have very good possibilities to agree about certain corrections."
